prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in which memory, the body and cosmology are fused into a singular metaphysical imaginative architecture

statement.case_for: My opening first choice holds after reading the colleagues' arguments. Judged on the common criteria, Cărtărescu's voice is among the most recognisable on the shortlist. In the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid, the body, childhood memory, dream and cosmology are built into one recursive structure, and the lyric foundation from his poetry is audible in the prose. The imaginative and intellectual depth does not rest on a single peak: it has been extended across several decades and several very large books. The case also has a clear attributable scope, one writer in Romanian, with the metaphysical novel project at the centre and poetry as its origin. I treat the fact that colleagues' first choices overlap as neither evidence nor reassurance. The case has to stand on voice, form and sustained depth, and I think it does. I rest this on public knowledge of the works, not on claimed direct reading or independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement is tied to dense Romanian wordplay, rhythm and patterning, and a committee working largely through translation may be judging a flattened version. The very large scale and recurrent motifs could also be read as insularity or repetition rather than deepening, and some long books may be uneven in control. If the committee cannot establish that the translated prose carries the stylistic achievement, then a more compressed oeuvre such as Michon's, or a more radically formal one such as Can Xue's, might be the safer choice. Even those are open to the same translation concern.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Michon second for exceptional linguistic and formal achievement in compressed French prose, and accepts that his smallness means the case rests on intensity rather than breadth.
responses.response: I agree on the quality of Small Lives and The Eleven, and it is why I keep Michon as my first alternative. I would qualify the claim that the compactness is mainly a strength. The criterion of sustained achievement across a body of work is harder to demonstrate for a slim corpus. The achievement also lives largely in French syntax and cadence, so the translation loss is probably larger than for Cărtărescu, whose effect depends more on large-scale architecture and imagery that survive translation better. That is a judgment about the type of effect, not a claim to have verified the translations.

responses.point: Sward ranks Can Xue second, arguing that the dream-logic strangeness is a deliberate method with its own internal rigor and few parallels in world literature, and she also notes that only part of the oeuvre is available in translation.
responses.response: I share the view that Can Xue's strangeness is method and not ornament, and I ranked her third. My reservation is the one Sward herself names: with limited translation coverage and few translators, we cannot tell whether the method develops or merely repeats across many books. A prize for the whole oeuvre needs evidence of variation and deepening, and for Cărtărescu the evidence is somewhat stronger because the large novels show a widening project. I would keep Can Xue as a serious alternative and would want closer discussion of how the translated selection represents the whole.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita second, seeing in Purgatory and Anteparadise a distinctive poetic language that turns historical suffering into collective memorial form, while flagging that non-textual interventions and political significance must not substitute for literary merit.
responses.response: I accept the caution Olsson raises himself, and I ranked Zurita sixth for the same reason. The formal ambition and scale are real, but the case would have to be made through the language of the poems. The landscape-scale and visual works are not wholly literary, and the translated poetry is the weakest basis for a judgment. Historical weight is a reason to read him closely, not a reason to rank him above a writer whose literary case is easier to make from the page.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson second for remaking the boundaries between classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and visual form, but notes that a citation would need careful articulation within Nobel's will and that some effects are bound to the book as a physical object.
responses.response: I put Carson fourth, and I think her reservations are the right ones. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real formal invention and an unmistakable intelligence. But a significant part of the achievement sits in book design, translation and classical scholarship, which are at the edge of an oeuvre-based literary assessment. I would want the committee to be able to name the core literary contribution, for example the hybrid lyric-essay form, before treating her as a laureate-level alternative to a writer whose achievement is carried more fully by the text.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement in dense, patterned Romanian prose and poetry survives in the translations available to the committee.
Whether the recurrent motifs and very large scale of his major novels represent deepening or repetition across the whole oeuvre.
Coverage of his poetry and early work in translation is uneven, and I have not independently verified any text.
Whether Michon's compact corpus and Can Xue's partly translated, method-driven corpus offer enough evidence of breadth and development to rival a larger body of work.
I rely on public knowledge of the works and on the colleagues' stated assessments, not on direct reading.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My background in fiction, Lagerlöf scholarship and my stated affinity with a British storytelling tradition give no documented tie to any shortlisted writer, and my own literary practice is context, not evidence of preference.
